opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's actually one of the most important shifts that has to happen, and honestly it's underappreciated. Right now there's a strange tension. People are already handing AI systems incredibly personal information: their health questions, their finances, their relationship problems, their company's internal documents. At the same time, there's a background unease, because you don't really know where that data goes. Is it being logged? Is it used for training? Who at the company can see it? Could it be subpoenaed? Most people just accept that trade-off because the utility is so high.

But I think that ceiling on trust is real, and it limits what AI can become. If you want an AI that actually acts on your behalf, that knows your full context, your emails, your medical history, your financial situation, and can make decisions for you, you have to give it everything. Rationally, people shouldn't do that with a system where the only guarantee is a privacy policy that can change next quarter.

So the way I think about confidentiality is moving from "trust us" to "verify it." With things like confidential computing and secure enclaves on modern GPUs, you can run inference so that even the operator of the hardware can't see what's being processed. You get cryptographic attestation showing exactly which model and code are running and that your data is encrypted in use. That changes the conversation. It's no longer about whether you believe a company's promises. It's a property of the system.

I think once that becomes the default, you'll see a big unlock. Enterprises with sensitive data that won't touch hosted models today, hospitals, banks, legal firms, will be able to use them. Individuals will be more comfortable letting an agent hold their full context. And it opens up new models of ownership, where your data and your AI's memory belong to you, not to a platform that monetizes it.

So confidentiality isn't just a nice privacy feature. It's a prerequisite for AI to work for the user rather than for whoever runs the servers. That's a big part of what we mean by user-owned AI.

r001.rationale: The response says most people accept the privacy trade-off and that individuals may become more comfortable, but does not state that people’s willingness threshold varies across individuals.

r002.rationale: It says confidential computing can prevent the hardware operator from seeing data and shift trust from promises to verifiable system properties. It does not clearly say this prevents any third party from accessing the data or removes an individual’s sharing threshold.

r003.rationale: The response describes secure enclaves and encrypted inference but does not compare their security with running AI locally.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the most underappreciated pieces of the whole picture right now. If you look at how people interact with AI today, there's this implicit bargain where you type your most sensitive stuff into a chat box, your health questions, your financial situation, your relationship problems, and you just kind of hope that whoever is running the model is being responsible with it. And most people don't really think about it, but when they do think about it, they get uncomfortable. We see this constantly with enterprises. A company wants to use a model on their internal documents, on customer data, and the legal team says, wait, where does this go, who can see it, is it being used for training. And that conversation stalls a lot of projects.

So the way I think about confidentiality is that it changes the question from "do I trust this company" to "do I even need to trust this company." Those are really different things. Trust in the first sense is about policies and terms of service and reputation, and that can change overnight, someone gets acquired, the privacy policy gets updated, there's a breach. Confidentiality in the second sense, when it's done with things like confidential computing, trusted execution environments, cryptographic attestation, means the operator literally cannot see your data even if they wanted to. The model runs on your inputs, you get the output, and nobody in the middle gets to look. You can verify that rather than just believe it.

And what's interesting is this is not a new idea, it's basically what we learned from the internet. Nobody would do online banking if we were still sending passwords in plaintext. HTTPS didn't make people trust banks more, it removed a whole category of trust that was required. I think AI is going to go through the same transition. Right now we're kind of in the plaintext era of AI, and I think a few years from now people will look back and find it strange that we were just sending everything to a server and hoping.

The other thing I'd say is this really matters for the kind of AI we're going to get. If the only way to use a powerful model is to hand your data to one of three or four big companies, then that's where all the data concentrates, and that concentration is itself a problem for the ecosystem, for competition, for user agency. If you can have confidential inference, then it becomes much more reasonable to have many providers, open models running in verifiable environments, and users actually owning their context, their history, their preferences, and bringing that to whichever model they want. So for me confidentiality isn't just about privacy as a nice-to-have, it's kind of the foundation for a more open and user-owned version of AI.

r001.rationale: The response says people become uncomfortable when they think about sharing sensitive data, but does not say the sensitivity threshold varies across individuals.

r002.rationale: It says confidentiality can change the question from whether users trust the company to whether they need to trust it, because the operator cannot see their data and this is verifiable.

r003.rationale: The response discusses confidential inference and verifiable environments but does not compare their security with running AI locally.

astra-6.text:
I think confidentiality changes the tradeoff quite a bit. Today, if you want an AI system to be really useful to you, you might need to give it access to your email, your documents, your calendar—quite a lot of your life. And then the question is, who else has access to that information? Is it the company running the model? Can it be used for training? Can somebody get access to it later?

If you can give people verifiable guarantees that their data is only being used for the computation they authorized, that makes a much more personal assistant possible. It can have the context to help you without requiring you to hand over that context for other purposes.

But confidentiality is one part of trust. You also need control over what the assistant can do. Reading your calendar and sending an email on your behalf are different permissions. So I think the opportunity is to combine confidentiality with that control, making it clear that the AI is working for you and that you decide what it can access and act on.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses the amount of personal context an assistant may need, but does not say that willingness to share varies across individuals.

r002.rationale: It describes guarantees that data is used only for authorized computation, but does not state that no third party can access the data or that this removes a user's sharing threshold.

r003.rationale: The candidate makes no comparison between confidential AI systems and running AI locally.

sol-6.1.text:
I think confidentiality changes the relationship quite a bit. Today, when you give an AI system access to your email or your documents, you’re also trusting the company operating that system. You’re trusting that they won’t use that information in a way you didn’t intend, and that nobody else will get access to it.

If you can provide a system where the data stays private, where you can verify that only the computation you authorized is happening, then you don’t need to make that same leap of faith. You can give an assistant more context, and that context is what makes it useful. It can understand what you’re working on, what your preferences are, and help you make decisions.

But confidentiality alone isn’t enough. You also need control over what the AI can do with that information. Reading my calendar and sending an email on my behalf are different permissions. So I think the opportunity is to combine privacy with clear boundaries, so people can get the benefit of a personal assistant without giving up control over their digital lives.

r001.rationale: It discusses trusting a company with personal data, but does not say that individuals differ in how sensitive data must be before they refuse to share it.

r002.rationale: It says private data and verifiable authorized computation reduce the need for a leap of faith, but does not state that confidentiality prevents any third party from accessing the data or removes the user's sharing threshold.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison between confidential AI systems and running AI locally.
